## Why not just draw a line through the gap? {#interpolation .split}

::: {.kicker}
Interpolation works under very restrictive set of assumptions.
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::: {.chart}
```{r}
lecture_chart("interpolation")
```
:::

::: explanation
- The post-crisis endpoint is already affected.
- A pre-crisis trend assumes growth would have continued unchanged.
- Neither uses evidence about shocks Ukraine would still have faced.

These dashed lines are illustrations.
:::

:::


::: {.source-links}
[World Bank WDI, saved 15 Nov 2026](https://data.worldbank.org/country/ukraine)
:::

::: {.notes}
Distinguish interpolation from extrapolation. Joining pre- and post-crisis actual outcomes is interpolation using an already-treated endpoint. Extending the earlier slope is extrapolation and assumes that slope would have continued. Neither identifies the no-crisis outcome. The chart intentionally shows both temptations. Do not say that a more complex method eliminates assumptions; it replaces a simple unsupported trajectory with a comparison whose assumptions can be examined.
:::

[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616) · [Author replication package, version 1, CC BY 4.0](https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/9bwk589xz6/1)
:::

::: {.notes}
This plot uses actual country observations from the authors' frozen 1995–2017 CSV, indexed to 2012 for comparability of movements. It is not a set of fitted placebos. Ukraine is highlighted; other lines are possible comparisons. Indexing can hide level differences, which is why the actual paper matches outcome levels and covariates as well. Shared exposure is useful only if it is not spillover from the treatment itself.
:::

## Build one comparison from pieces of several countries. {#idea .method}

::: {.kicker}
Synthetic control is a weighted comparison
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::::: {.method-steps}
::: {.method-step}
[Before the crisis]{.method-stage}

**Find a blend that tracks Ukraine.**

Use earlier output and relevant characteristics to choose the proportions.
:::

::: {.method-step}
[At the boundary]{.method-stage}

**Freeze the proportions.**

Do not use post-crisis outcomes to choose the blend.
:::

::: {.method-step}
[After the crisis]{.method-stage}

**Compare the paths.**

Ask whether the divergence is unusual and whether the comparison is credible.
:::
:::::

::: {.method-chart .period-strip}
1995–2012: choose weights → 
2013: freeze weights → 
2013–2017: compare outcomes
:::

:::


::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616)
:::

::: {.notes}
No equations are needed. Weights are nonnegative and add to 100%. They represent a statistical comparison, not ownership, trade shares, or a claim that Ukraine is literally made of these countries. Pre-treatment matching and validation are not a guarantee against post-treatment confounding. Only the method diagram is schematic on this slide; it is not an estimator result.
:::

## From regression to synthetic control {#synthetic-formula}

::: {.kicker}
Fit Ukraine using two comparison countries before the crisis
:::

::: {.slide-content .formula-content}
::: {.formula-line}
OLS: $\displaystyle \min_{\beta_1,\beta_2}\; \sum_{t \leq 2012} \left(y_t - \beta_1 x_{1t} - \beta_2 x_{2t}\right)^2$
:::

::: {.formula-explain}
$y_t$: Ukraine’s GDP per person; $x_{1t}$ and $x_{2t}$: donor countries’ GDP per person.
:::

::: {.fragment .formula-step}
**1. Synthetic-control restrictions:** $\beta_1 \geq 0, \quad \beta_2 \geq 0, \quad \beta_1 + \beta_2 = 1$.

The coefficients become nonnegative weights that sum to one.
:::

::: {.fragment .formula-step}
**2. Regularization (optional):** add $\displaystyle \lambda\left(\beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2\right)$, where $\lambda \geq 0$.

This ridge penalty discourages large coefficients.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
This is a simplified two-donor illustration, without an intercept. The objective fits pre-crisis outcomes only; the fitted weights are then held fixed after 2012. Adding the ridge penalty creates a penalized variant, not a necessary step in standard synthetic control. Actual implementations may match additional predictors and weight them differently, as in the paper.
:::

## A synthetic Ukraine, 1995 to 2017. {#paper .paper}

::: {.kicker}
Bluszcz & Valente · Defence and Peace Economics · 2022
:::

::: {.slide-content}
:::::: paper-design
::: {}
[18]{.design-number}

countries\
Ukraine + 17 possible donors
:::

::: {}
[414]{.design-number}

country-year observations\
in the public data
:::

::: {}
[2013]{.design-number}

first treated year\
in the authors\' design
:::
::::::

::::: period-strip
::: {}
Fit on 1995--2012
:::

::: {}
Evaluate 2013--2017
:::
:::::

Outcome: real GDP **per person**, in 2011 international dollars at PPP.

The design covers the broader crisis beginning in 2013, not the isolated effect of fighting in 2014 or the invasion in 2022.

:::

::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616) · [Author replication package, version 1, CC BY 4.0](https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/9bwk589xz6/1)
:::

::: {.notes}
The original paper uses five averaged predictors plus GDP-per-capita values in 2000 and 2012, fitting on 1995–2012. Explain PPP simply as a common purchasing-power unit rather than market-exchange-rate dollars. The public files have 414 observations, 18 countries, 23 years. Four donors have substantial published weights. A local rerun of the national model reproduces the published rounded weights and headline shortfall.
:::

## The paper's headline: a shortfall against the counterfactual. {#gap .split}

::: {.kicker}
Published Table 5 · national rerun matches to two decimal places
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::: {.chart}
```{r}
lecture_chart("published-gap")
```
:::

:::: explanation
::: {.big-stat .negative}
15.1%
:::

average GDP-per-person shortfall\
for 2013--2017 · reproduced in our rerun

Not a 15.1% fall from the previous year.

Not an estimate of the contribution of lost trade alone.
::::

:::

::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616)
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the bars as the percentage by which observed GDP per person is below the authors' synthetic counterfactual in each year. The paper's Table 5 reports 5.23%, 9.18%, 19.63%, 19.80%, and 21.67%, averaging 15.10%. The blue line graph on the previous slide is a rounded-weight reconstruction; these bars transcribe the published table. The independent rerun matches each annual percentage to two decimal places and gives a mean of 15.103%. The paper's average dollar gap is 1,438.90 international 2011 dollars per person. These are model-based estimates, not observed accounting losses.
:::

## What happens when an important donor is removed? {#sensitivity .split}

::: {.kicker}
Published leave-one-out results · average annual shortfall per person
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::: {.chart}
```{r}
lecture_chart("sensitivity")
```
:::

::: explanation
The paper refits the model after removing each positive-weight donor.

The shortfall remains, but its size changes.

This does not settle regional spillovers, concurrent shocks, or changing statistical coverage.

Removing both Moldova and Armenia is a further check, not a result shown here.
:::

:::

::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616)
:::

::: {.notes}
This chart redraws the paper's published Table 4, not our refitted estimates. Our Armenia exclusion gives 1,754.99 rather than the published 1,737.9; the cause is unresolved. Original average shortfall 1,438.9; removing Slovenia 1,501.0; Bulgaria 1,666.4; Armenia 1,737.9; Moldova 1,587.4, all in 2011 PPP dollars per person. The paper does not show a joint exclusion of Moldova and Armenia in this table. Do not replace a refit by mechanically renormalizing fixed published weights and call it a leave-one-out replication. The numbers here show larger shortfalls after each exclusion, not a disappearance of the result.
:::

## Would the same method find a crisis in the donor countries? {#placebos .placebos}

::: {.kicker}
Give each donor the same pretend intervention date
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::: {.placebo-countries}
### 1 treated country + 17 donor comparisons

```{r}
#| results: asis
cat("**Ukraine** · ", paste(names(lecture_data$donors), collapse = " · "), "\n\n", sep = "")
```

Procedure illustration. No new placebo estimates are shown.
:::

::: explanation
1.  Build a synthetic comparison for each donor.
2.  Check its fit before 2013.
3.  Compare the later divergence with Ukraine\'s.

With few comparisons, inference is coarse. Different pre-fit rules and statistics give different rankings.
:::

:::

::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616)
:::

::: {.notes}
The country dots illustrate the placebo procedure; they are not a fresh set of fitted placebo paths or observed test statistics. The paper reports several different summaries: ATT ranking after six pre-fit exclusions gives 1/12, about 8.3%; the post/pre squared-error ranking gives 2/18, about 11.1%; its joint ATT–MPE comparison reports 1/18 while calling it significant at 5%. One over eighteen is about 5.6%, not below 5%. Do not turn these distinct criteria into one interchangeable p-value or present placebo ranks as randomized assignment probabilities without assumptions. We reran placebo fits, but have not verified the paper's inference conventions; no new placebo estimates are shown here.
:::

## A replication should expose the choices. {#replication .replication}

::: {.kicker}
What we reproduced, and what still needs checking
:::

::: {.slide-content}
::::: replication-columns
::: {}
### National model rerun

- Headline shortfall reproduced: 15.103%.
- Annual gaps and major weights match published rounding.
- Placebos and donor exclusions refitted.
- Charts still display published values or rounded-weight reconstruction.
:::

::: {}
### Still to check

- Investigate the Armenia exclusion discrepancy.
- Verify placebo inference conventions.
- Reproduce regional and remaining robustness results.
- Test donor-pool and treatment-date choices.
:::
:::::

National headline replicated to reported precision. Full paper replication remains incomplete.

:::

::: {.source-links}
[Bluszcz & Valente, Defence and Peace Economics, 2022](https://doi.org/10.1080/10242694.2020.1791616) · [Author replication package, version 1, CC BY 4.0](https://data.mendeley.com/datasets/9bwk589xz6/1)
:::

::: {.notes}
The original R script references two absent columns in unused preprocessing lines, and the implemented trade-dependence measure is GDP-based rather than the paper's verbal trade-share description. The teaching rerun documents these changes. It matches the headline and annual gaps to published precision. Removing Armenia gives 1,754.99 versus the published 1,737.9 international dollars; the difference remains unexplained. Placebo inference and regional results remain unchecked. The national data are frozen historical observations; swapping in today's WDI data is an extension, not an exact reproduction.
:::
